scenes.title: Publish and filter SNS messages
scenes.narration: The recovered architecture shows one SNS topic with two subscriptions and different filter policies. A publisher emits messages with a severity attribute. The Lambda remediation subscription accepts only critical events, while the SQS audit subscription accepts critical and informational events. Trace the arrows: critical messages are delivered to both subscriptions, but informational messages reach only the audit queue. Filter policy scope matters: SNS can evaluate message attributes or message body fields when the subscription is configured appropriately. Inspect the sample publish messages and notification outputs rather than assuming a single global topic filter. The topic is a fan-out mechanism; each subscription controls which matching events it receives. Subscriber permissions, retries and idempotency remain relevant because delivery can fail or repeat. This pattern lets one event stream support rapid remediation and durable audit workflows without tightly coupling publishers to either consumer.  As you follow the recovered image, distinguish the request or event flow from the management and permission controls. Pay special attention to which operations are asynchronous, which are subject to retries, and what an operator should verify in AWS logs or the console before marking the workflow successful.

scenes.title: Send a direct mobile push notification
scenes.narration: The slide walks through mobile push delivery using Amazon SNS. First, the mobile application registers with Apple Push Notification service or Firebase Cloud Messaging and obtains a device token. Next, the backend creates an SNS platform endpoint associated with that token and obtains an endpoint ARN. The application can publish a message to the endpoint ARN, and SNS routes it through the applicable mobile push provider to the device. The bottom compares a direct endpoint publish for one device with publishing to a topic containing subscribed device endpoints for a group notification. Note the operational panel: device tokens can rotate, platform endpoints can become disabled, and the application should update its token-to-endpoint association and handle delivery errors. A platform endpoint is not the same thing as a user identity, so authentication and consent are application concerns.  As you follow the recovered image, distinguish the request or event flow from the management and permission controls. Pay special attention to which operations are asynchronous, which are subject to retries, and what an operator should verify in AWS logs or the console before marking the workflow successful.

scenes.title: Build an AppFlow transfer: source, trigger, destination
scenes.narration: This is a console-style Amazon AppFlow walkthrough for moving SaaS knowledge records to Amazon S3. Start by creating a flow and authenticating a supported source connector, illustrated with Salesforce. Select the source object and only the necessary fields, choose S3 as the destination and define bucket, prefix and file format. Then configure a run trigger: on demand, scheduled or event-driven where the particular connector supports it. The next panel maps source fields into destination fields and validates the flow; the final panel shows a successful run and the resulting S3 location. The sample JSON record demonstrates how fields such as identifiers, title, summary and content can be prepared for later AI indexing. Connector capabilities, trigger types and supported transformations vary, so verify the selected connector rather than treating every dropdown option as universally available. Protect source credentials, data permissions and downstream ingestion access.  As you follow the recovered image, distinguish the request or event flow from the management and permission controls. Pay special attention to which operations are asynchronous, which are subject to retries, and what an operator should verify in AWS logs or the console before marking the workflow successful.

scenes.title: Tune SQS queue behavior and inspect output
scenes.narration: The final recovered slide is a hands-on SQS operations walkthrough. Create a standard queue, then configure retention, visibility timeout, delivery delay and message-size constraints according to the workload. Attach a dead-letter queue with a maximum receive count so repeatedly failing messages are isolated for investigation. The example sends a small job message with an S3 reference, receives it, processes the task and deletes it on success. If the worker does not delete the message and it becomes visible again, repeated failed receives eventually move it to the dead-letter queue. Use the lower status tables to distinguish available messages from in-flight messages and see the DLQ entry after repeated failure. Treat displayed default and maximum values as settings shown in the example, and verify service limits for the actual deployment. A DLQ does not solve the underlying failure, but makes it observable and recoverable.
